papers.title: SpectroBird: Event-Level Vocalization Detection and Curation for Avian Ecology
papers.abstract: Passive acoustic monitoring often summarizes long recordings as fixed-window presence predictions, but many ecological questions require records of individual vocal events: how many occurred, when they occurred, whether they overlapped, how long they lasted, what frequency band they occupied, and whether each event was complete enough for structural measurement. We address this event-level measurement problem with SpectroBird, a spectrogram-based method for localizing and curating avian vocalizations in noisy field recordings. SpectroBird first applies a detection-localization model to identify candidate vocalizations as time-frequency boxes. An event-consolidation step merges repeated detections from overlapping windows while preserving overlapping vocalizations as separate events. A completeness-curation model then classifies each consolidated event as complete or incomplete before downstream event-level analysis. We demonstrate SpectroBird on breeding-season Hume's Leaf Warbler buzz vocalizations recorded in the Himalaya across a 3,200-3,800 m elevational gradient. Under shared window-level scoring, the detection-localization model remained competitive with AST and YOLOv11-cls baselines while retaining event timing and frequency bounds; event-level evaluation achieved AP > 0.999 for complete buzzes. Applied to two field seasons, the resulting event records showed that duration of complete buzzes declined with elevation, complete-buzz occurrence showed no simple elevation trend, and relative day-of-year occurrence patterns were strongly correlated between years. These results show how event-level detection and curation can support ecological analyses that depend on individual vocalizations rather than fixed-window presence alone.

papers.title: SLAFIT: Viral fitness inference and structural variant detection from TGS data
papers.abstract: Evolution is driven by genetic variation at multiple scales, from single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) to structural variants (SVs). Within populations, nonrandom associations among SNVs, quantified by linkage disequilibrium (LD), must be considered when inferring fitness from sequencing data. Characterizing SVs, SNVs, and the LD between SNVs therefore provides complementary insights into the genetic basis of evolutionary change. Although third-generation sequencing technologies facilitate the characterization of genomic variation, finite read lengths often limit the resolution of LD across entire genomes. Here, we present SLAFIT, a pipeline for linkage-aware fitness inference and SV detection from third-generation sequencing data. The pipeline reconstructs genome-wide haplotypes and their frequencies from third-generation sequencing reads to infer SNVs and estimate LD. When time-series data are available, it also infers fitness. An established SV detection tool is incorporated into the same workflow. Simulations support accurate LD and fitness inference under tested conditions, with reduced computation time through parallelization. Applications to enterovirus C104 and herpes simplex virus 1 reveal selection signals in predicted epitopes and recover a known inversion, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of SLAFIT for studying viral evolution through complementary analyses of fitness and structural variation.

papers.title: The (implicit) force is with you: an application of the implicit function theorem for automatic protein force fields reparametrization
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics simulations are powerful tools for studying protein behavior, yet their accuracy remains limited by the approximations of molecular force fields and the difficulty of determining their parameters. Moreover, existing force fields are largely optimized for globular proteins and can perform poorly on structurally distinct systems. Developing a universal force field that accurately describes all existing protein structures may be beyond reach with current physical models. Instead, we propose shifting generality from the force field itself to the method used to assign its parameters, enabling systematic reparameterization for restricted, structurally homogeneous classes of proteins. We formulate this task as a bilevel optimization problem and solve it using the implicit function theorem. We demonstrate this approach by reparameterizing AMBER for amyloid fibrils, optimizing its parameters to improve agreement with experimentally determined structures and enhance fibril stability during molecular dynamics simulations.

papers.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Assay-Aware Drug-Target Binding Affinity Prediction
papers.abstract: Machine learning models for molecular discovery often train on bioactivity data from heterogeneous assays, yet assay context is rarely explicitly represented. We investigate whether natural-language assay descriptions provide predictive information beyond molecular and protein representations. We develop ACL-DTI (Assay-aware Contrastive Learning-based Drug Target Interaction) and MAMMAL-AsAP, an assay-context extension of MAMMAL-DTI. Across five triplet-disjoint random splits, assay-aware models achieve competitive or improved performance over assay-agnostic baselines. Among the evaluated models, MAMMAL-AsAP achieves the highest (R^2) of 0.7198 +/- 0.0085. Masking experiments show that ACL-DTI is robust to incomplete assay descriptions, exhibiting the smallest reductions in R^2 among the evaluated models when masking the target name, assay technique, or both: 0.0228 +/- 0.0064, 0.0406 +/- 0.0113, and 0.0620 +/- 0.0190, respectively. These results indicate that assay descriptions contain predictive information not fully captured by molecular structures and protein sequences, and reveal architecture-dependent differences in how this information is exploited.

papers.title: BioMINTREL expands biological problem solving through cross-disciplinary representations
papers.abstract: Biological research agents often rely on familiar analytical methods, limiting the questions explored in existing data. We introduce BioMINTREL, an AI agent that finds methods from other disciplines and connects them to biological measurements. It can draw on relationships among datasets and complementary ideas from several methods to develop new questions and analyses. We evaluate it on BioMDC-Bench, which assesses 228 possible applications of computational methods to biological tasks. Compared with GPT-5.4 mini and Qwen3.6-35B, BioMINTREL improves F1 agreement with human experts by up to 45.3 percentage points and increases coverage of applications supported by studies published in subsequent years by up to 58.8 percentage points. Four case studies on real data go beyond previous analyses to reveal dose-specific variant effects, constraints on spatial cell communication and routes through perturbation-response states, and identify the sampling needed to test whether rare high-state cells predict later lineage size. These results highlight BioMINTREL's potential to expand questions in existing data and suggest directions for subsequent research.

papers.title: ELiAH2: update of the atlas of E3 ligases in human tissues by integrating tissue-specificity and docking properties of ligands for targeted protein degradation
papers.abstract: Targeted protein degradation (TPD), including proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), requires coordinated selection of E3 ligases, target proteins, and ligands to achieve efficient and tissue-selective degradation. However, current TPD resources provide limited support for integrating tissue-specific transcriptomic evidence with structural compatibility during early candidate prioritization. Here, we present ELiAH2, an expanded database for transcriptome- and structure-guided prioritization of TPD candidates. ELiAH2 integrates GTEx RNA-seq profiles across 24 human tissues to characterize tissue-specific expression patterns of E3 ligases and target genes. Compared with the previous version, ELiAH, current update presented over 200% of expansion for the number of covered tissues and samples. Previously, E3 ligase-target gene associations were inferred using mutual information-based network analysis, enabling users to explore transcriptomic relationships. To further support structural evaluation, ELiAH2 provides large-scale docking datasets comprising 827,385 E3 ligase-target protein pairs and 7,800,521 protein-ligand docking models, including E3 ligase-ligand and target protein-ligand interactions. Docking scores, ranked interaction tables, gene and ligand identifiers, and downloadable PDB structures are incorporated into the web interface. By combining tissue specificity, E3-target association, protein-protein docking, and protein-ligand docking, ELiAH2 provides a comprehensive resource for narrowing the TPD search space and supporting rational degrader design. ELiAH2 is freely available at https://eliahdb.org.

papers.title: MassBank Human: The annotated human metabolome
papers.abstract: Mass spectrometry-based metabolomics is essential for deciphering human metabolic functions and metabolite dark matter. However, the dark matter of the human metabolome is intricately hidden. Therefore, we developed MassBank Human, a curated library that distills 36,512,540 MS2 spectra from 76 public human datasets into 203,886 high-quality spectra via spectral averaging, recalibration, and filtering to achieve high mass accuracy. We further used three metabolite annotation tools and developed a Zipf-Bayesian rank aggregation framework to aggregate their rankings with false discovery rate control. This framework assigned molecular formulas, chemical classes, and planar structures to 55,564, 22,619, and 14,198 spectra, respectively. Approximately half of the annotated structures potentially originated from food, pollutants, or gut microbiota. In a metabolome analysis of colorectal cancer cells, MassBank Human doubled structural annotation coverage (10.6% to 21.2%), identifying acetylated polyamines as markers of metabolic rewiring. This community resource provides an annotated foundation for exploring human metabolomes.

papers.title: The Evolving Bileome: A Pan-Repository Landscape of Expanded Bile Acid and Related Steroidal Signatures
authors: J. J. J. van der Hooft
papers.abstract: Bile acids and related steroidal metabolites are among the most studied biomolecules, yet recent work has revealed far greater structural diversity than previously recognized, much of it shaped by the microbiome. We previously introduced a repository-scale bile acid MS/MS library built from queries targeting C24 bile acid fragmentation, limited to Orbitrap Q Exactive datasets within GNPS/MassIVE. Here we announce a major expansion of this library: a bile acid and steroidal MS/MS spectral library assembled across three major metabolomics repositories, now capturing C23, C24 (including alkamine), C26 (C-C bonded aceto derivatives), and C27 bile acids, as well as C28 bile alcohols. The expanded libraries comprise 640,141 unique MS/MS spectra, of which 120,293 (18.8%) match 2,529 reference spectra, leaving most of this steroidal chemical space structurally unassigned. Linked to harmonized pan-repository metadata, the library provides a starting point for classifying MS/MS spectra as likely bile acids or related steroids, with two example analyses illustrated here. This resource allows researchers to flag candidate bile acid and steroidal signatures in their own data for further characterization.

papers.title: Mechanism-guided Discovery of Fluoroacetate Dehalogenase (FAcD) Variants for Enzymatic PFAS Defluorination
papers.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent anthropogenic "forever chemicals" whose strong C-F bonds (~460-533 kJ mol-1) resist defluorination, and the recast EU Drinking Water Directive sets parametric values of 0.10 ug L-1 for the sum of 20 specified PFAS and 0.50 ug L-1 for total PFAS. Here, we present DeFluorX, a mechanism-first pipeline that uses Boltz-2 to co-fold 2,150 bacterial fluoroacetate dehalogenase (FAcD) variants with 26 PFAS and fluoroacetate, generating uniformly high model confidence (rho = +0.08) but poorly tracked catalytic competence. Thus, the complexes were ranked and tiered by SN2-defluorination geometry based on the known mechanism of control of FAcDs RPA1163 with fluoroacetate: Odelta...C-alpha distance and Odelta-C-alpha-F angle; relay; carboxylate clamp; F-stabiliser; F-cradle; and penalties for scissile bond strength, backside occlusion, beta-fluorination and bond multiplicity. The tiering identified eight complexes (med angle 173.2 degrees, distance 2.91 A) with a high probability of degradation, including Alphaproteobacterial enzymes, with mono-, di- and trifluoroacetate attacking at 172-178 degrees versus 163 degrees for the control. We performed WaterMap, restrained 1 us Desmond MD, MM-GBSA and scans of the three WaterMap-aware best MD frames per complex using B3LYP/6-31G** QM/MM. All 12 frames exhibited product-end C-F cleavage with barriers ranging from 1.1 to 11.8 kcal mol-1, and the departing fluoride carried -0.43 to -0.63 e. The Laboratory validation is ongoing.

papers.title: Modulator Resolves Transcript-, Allele-, and Condition-associated RNA Modification Differences from Direct RNA Sequencing
papers.abstract: Nanopore direct-RNA sequencing (DRS) reports RNA modifications on single molecules, but there is no comprehensive algorithm for processing, aligning, and differentiating base modifications across reads that are often 5'-truncated. Here we present Modulator, which assigns every read, truncated or not, to a fragmentform, defined by a shared transcript 3'-end and the splice-junctions upstream of it. Of note, Modulator builds fragmentforms from genomic alignments without a reference transcriptome, estimates per-base modification stoichiometry within each fragmentform, and classifies each stoichiometry difference as transcript-, allele-, or condition-dependent. In the control HG002 transcriptome, Modulator built 23,746 fragmentforms, with 15,620 candidate novel isoforms that carried poly(A) signals as often as previously annotated transcripts. Also, assigning 5'-truncated reads to fragmentforms nearly doubled the number of testable and differentially modified sites. m6A sites within 100 nucleotides (nt) of a splice junction or within 1 kb of a poly(A) site were less modified in fragmentforms that use that junction or poly(A) site, indicating that local transcript context shapes where m6A is deposited. From the same reads, Modulator called SNPs with 93% precision and no phasing errors against the Genome in a Bottle benchmark. It identified 131 SNPs that create or remove a modifiable nucleotide and 1,358 allele-specific modification differences, most involving SNPs more than 50 nt from the modified site. In cells infected with Zika virus, which remodels gene expression relative to uninfected cells, Modulator identified 1,253 transcript-independent modification stoichiometry changes. Of the m6A changes at sites measured by GLORI, 96% agreed in direction with single-nucleotide-resolution GLORI maps of the same samples. Thus, Modulator accurately separates changes in RNA modification from transcript-associated and allele-associated differences and can improve the utility of nanopore DRS. Availability and Implementation: Modulator is free and open source: https://github.com/Theo-Nelson/Modulator. It is written in Python and runs on Linux OS.

papers.title: The Multi-scale Copula Index (MCI): a new information-theoretic measure of association and its applications in functional cancer genomics
papers.abstract: Cancer genomic analyses increasingly involve large, complex datasets representing diverse omics variables, such as gene expression, mutations, copy number alterations, genetic perturbations (e.g. CRISPR or iRNA), drug sensitivity, and clinical phenotypes, making it crucial to accurately measure associations among these variables. Traditional correlation-based methods, like the Pearson correlation coefficient, often assume linearity, Gaussian distributions, and independence among variables, leading to oversimplified assumptions, less sensitive readouts and less accurate significance estimation. Information-theoretic measures overcome these limitations by being one step removed from the data and assessing dependencies at the level of probability distributions, thus providing a more data-agnostic, robust measure for identifying associations in common analysis tasks such as feature selection, pattern recognition, and predictive modeling. Building on these foundations, we introduce the Multi-scale Copula Index (MCI), a novel information-theoretic measure of association. The MCI offers significant advantages over existing methods by eliminating the need for density estimation and parameter tuning, thereby ensuring consistent estimation with reduced computational complexity. Furthermore, it enhances statistical power at lower sample sizes, exhibits strong robustness to outliers, and successfully captures both directionality and important symmetries under input-data transformations, such as reflection or complementation. Due to these strengths, the MCI is particularly useful for functional cancer genomic applications involving, e.g., transcriptional and perturbational data, with different statistical properties across a wide range of dataset sizes and complexity. Contextual associations often arise in functional genomics datasets: two genomic variables show little or no correlation in most samples, yet display a strong linkage within the subset that reflects the active biological context. These situations are ideal for quantifying associations with the MCI. We illustrate the performance of the MCI in a variety of benchmarks and cancer genomic examples and applications. We also introduce the Cumulative Entropy Diagram (CED), a graphical display that allows the visualization of the MCI between a reference vector, such as a phenotype, pathway activation or drug response, and a complete set of genomic features.

papers.title: In Silico Design and Comprehensive Evaluation of a Novel Multi-Epitope Vaccine Candidate Against Chandipura Virus
papers.abstract: Chandipura virus (CHPV), an emerging arthropod-borne member of the Rhabdovirdae family, is an acute neurotropic pathogen responsible for explosive outbreak of acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) predominantly in pediatric cohorts. with mortality rates exceeding 70%, seizures, and death within 24 to 48 hours. the complete lack of approved antiviral therapies or preventive vaccine makes this a severe global health threat. to address this ,our study utilized a computational reverse vaccinology approach to design and structurally evaluate a novel epitope-based vaccine construct. and computationally validate a 104-amino-acid chimeric peptide vaccine candidate targeting immunoinformatics screening confirmed that the construct possesses strong predicted protective antigencity (VaxiJen >0.40) complete absence of allergenicity across multiple machine-learning models (AllerTopv2.0 and AllergenFP v1.0),and zero cellular or hemolytic toxicity (ToxinPred SVM regression score < 0.0). physicochemical characterization via EXPASY ProtParam established an 11.76 kDa construct comprising 1,653 atoms, with a theoretical isoelectric point of 7.78 an instability index of 39.92 (classifying the protein as physically stable), an aliphatic index of 81.73, and a grand average of Hydropathicity (GRAVY) of -0.350. These values confirm the construct is highly soluble in aqueous environments, which is necessary for physiological delivery. to prepare for expression, the sequence was reverse translated by codon-optimized for escherichia coli strain K12. JCat analysis returned a codonasaptation index (CAI) of 0.956 alongside of GC content of 61.48%. Subsequent in silico cloning successfully placed the 315 bp expression cassette into the pET-28a(+) vector, directly downstream of the T7 promoter. next, we evaluated receptor interaction by docking the construct against human Toll-Like Receptor 4 (TLR4;PDB ID: 4G8A). Using Hawkrank score of -5845.39 We validated this affinity with MM/GBSA calculations, which revealed a strong net binding free energy ({Delta}Gbind) of -29.12 kcal/mol, because static dicking cannot account for molecular flexibility, we then performed normal mode analysis (NMA) via the iMODS server. this dynamic simulation demonstrated structural stability throughout the construct was analyzed. The analysis found a fundamental eigenvalue of 4.62422*10-. the covariance matrix and elastic network showed highly correlated residue motions. to predict the vaccine's effectiveness we ran a 70-day simulation with C-Immsim. the data showed antigen clearance along with a strong primary IgM response successfully changed into IgG1 and IgG2 antibodies levels. The model also predicted an increase in active helper T cells. it also showed production of Th1 cytokines (inf-{gamma} and IL-2). this computer result prove the immune health of the chandipura virus construct. they give a reason to move this candidate forward for recombinants expression and in vivo preclinical testing.

papers.title: CucurbitAgent: An AI agent for exploring cucurbit multi-omics resources
papers.abstract: Functional genomics in crops increasingly depends on integrating information from an extensive literature and heterogeneous multi-omics datasets. Large language models (LLMs) offer a powerful approach to synthesizing these resources and revealing hidden connections across datasets; however, they frequently hallucinate, producing plausible but unsupported claims, when responding to gene-specific queries. Here, we present CucurbitAgent, an AI research agent for functional genomics in the Cucurbitaceae, a major family of horticultural crops. CucurbitAgent integrates multi-omics resources from nine cultivated cucurbit species and more than 18,000 publications, encompassing approximately 256,000 genes, tissue-resolved expression profiles, over 16 million natural genetic variants, and roughly 242,000 predicted protein structures with more than 14 million predicted binding-site residue annotations. Responses link retrieved evidence to source records, including gene entries, expression measurements, structural predictions, and literature passages. On a curated benchmark of 50 tasks assessed by domain experts under blinded conditions, CucurbitAgent achieved an overall pairwise win rate of 96.0% against nine general-purpose LLMs, based on weighted scores for factual accuracy, completeness, relevance, and traceability. The platform is freely available at https://cucurbitagent.com and supports queries in 37 languages collectively spoken by an estimated 70% or more of the world's population. CucurbitAgent not only unifies evidence retrieval and interpretation but also reveals latent associations across datasets, helping researchers formulate testable hypotheses and substantially accelerating candidate-gene research. Its framework is readily transferable to other crops and, more broadly, provides a blueprint for building specialized agents in any domain.

papers.title: Evaluating Nanopore read trimming and quality filtering in bacterial genomics
papers.abstract: Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) sequencing is widely used in bacterial genomics, particularly for reference-based variant calling and de novo assembly. Both analyses routinely start with quality control (QC) preprocessing, but as ONT basecalling accuracy has improved, its necessity and downstream trade-offs remain poorly defined. We benchmarked 17 preprocessing combinations, built from three adapter trimmers (Dorado, Porechop_ABI, Barbell) and three quality-based processing tools (Filtlong, Chopper, SeqKit) with untrimmed and unprocessed controls, plus Fastplong, which performs both. Each combination was evaluated across 13 bacterial isolates at 100x and 20x depth under the HAC and SUP basecalling models. Variant calling was assessed by F1 score. Assemblies were scored on sequence accuracy, contiguity, replicon recovery and residual adapter contamination, then aggregated into a weighted arithmetic mean using weights from a survey of the microbial genomics community. With SUP basecalling, raw reads with no trimming or quality-based processing produced accurate SNP calls and outperformed several pipelines that applied both operations; adapter trimming alone left SNP accuracy unchanged. Subsetting reads by combined length and quality with Filtlong gave the highest SNP F1 scores at both depths, except with Barbell at 20x, where it ranked second lowest. As is often the case in benchmarking studies, assembly results involved trade-offs, and the best tool depends on which aspects of performance matter most for a given use. Filtlong produced the lowest error rates, but every Filtlong pipeline lost three small plasmids at both depths. Barbell trimming raised error rates and reduced contiguity at 20x, while skipping adapter trimming left residual adapter and barcode sequences in assemblies. Under the community-derived weights, Porechop_ABI followed by Chopper had the highest overall score at both depths, without winning any single metric. QC tool choice should therefore be guided by the downstream analysis goal rather than applied indiscriminately across all workflows.

papers.title: IsoMatch enables population-scale transcript integration and reveals reference-dependent isoform novelty
papers.abstract: Transcriptome analyses increasingly generate large collections of transcript models that must be integrated, compared and interpreted across samples and reference annotations. Transcript novelty depends on structural equivalence criteria and reference annotation. Here we present IsoMatch, a scalable framework that harmonizes transcript merging and reference-based classification through explicit, configurable structural criteria. IsoMatch preserves source-GTF and original-transcript traceability throughout the workflow, allowing every merged and classified model to be traced back to its contributing inputs. Benchmarking showed that IsoMatch preserves distinct transcript models during integration through configurable matching parameters for both splice junction chains and transcript ends. With its index-based architecture, IsoMatch merged 163 ENCODE transcript catalogs and classified 7.9 million transcript models with peak memory usage of 0.49 GB and 1.1 GB, respectively. Integrating GENCODE, RefSeq and CHESS revealed that 71.2% of transcript groups remained annotation-specific even without terminal constraints. For 4.84 million merged transcript models from 119 long-read transcriptomes from the 1000 Genomes Project, the integrated reference increased the full-splice match proportion from 12.0-13.6% with individual annotations to 18.0%. IsoMatch enables scalable transcript integration and classification with explicit structural criteria and preserved traceability, demonstrating how reference choice shapes estimates of transcript novelty.

papers.title: NeoOmni Atlas: an integrated database for pan-cancer neoantigen derived from proteogenomics analysis
papers.abstract: Tumor neoantigens derived from diverse molecular aberrations are important targets for personalized cancer immunotherapy, but existing resources incompletely integrate mass-spectrometry-supported canonical and non-canonical antigen evidence across cancer types. NeoOmni Atlas is an interactive pan-cancer T-cell epitope resource, built via proteogenomic reanalysis of 7,561 immunopeptidomics datasets comprising 511 million raw spectra from 2,341 samples across 26 cancer types. The analysis yielded 872,414 eluted canonical peptides and 198,961 non-canonical peptides spanning 18 molecular alteration classes, along with 759,386 unique ligands presented by 322 human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles. Relative to existing repositories, NeoOmni Atlas covers a broader range of cancer types, includes 60 additional HLA alleles, and catalogs 369,781 novel ligands. A computational tumor-specific filtering framework identified 316,126 tumor-associated epitopes and 61,231 tumor-specific epitopes. Tumor-specific epitopes showed stronger predicted binding affinity than tumor-associated epitopes for HLA class I A and B alleles, and 65 conserved tumor-specific epitopes recurrent across more than 10 tumor types represent potential shared antigen candidates. NeoOmni Atlas also prioritizes candidate tumor-associated antigens including PMEL (gp100:209-217) and CSPG4, and supports browsing, searching, and downloading by cancer type, human leukocyte antigen allele, peptide sequence, and source event. NeoOmni Atlas is freely accessible at http://modinfor.com/NeoOmni-Atlas/.

papers.title: Antigen-aware TCR embeddings reveal conserved immune patterns for personalized immune monitoring
papers.abstract: T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires are highly individualized, while technical variation further complicates comparisons across individuals and cohorts. Here, we present TCRmeta, an antigen-aware framework that integrates population-scale repertoire relationships with experimentally defined antigen specificity to establish a shared space for repertoire analysis. TCRmeta predicted mutation-induced changes and captured antigen-related relationships in TCR specificity. Despite extensive sequence diversity, TCRmeta revealed a conserved repertoire landscape, enabling construction of a healthy reference for quantifying repertoire dispersal. Across cohorts, aging was associated with conserved V gene changes and progressive dispersal, with greater dispersal in CMV-positive individuals. Longitudinal analysis showed that repertoires progressively shifted toward the healthy reference following bone marrow transplantation or antiretroviral therapy. To directly compare repertoires in TCRmeta space, we developed Energy Shift, a pairwise measure robust to technical variation and HLA background while remaining sensitive to biological differences. Together, TCRmeta enables quantitative cross-individual and longitudinal immune monitoring.

papers.title: Immunoinformatics-Based Design of a Chimeric Vaccine Against Necator americanus Targeting the Na-APR-1, Na-GST-1, and Na-ASP-2 Vaccine Candidates
papers.abstract: Hookworm infection, caused predominantly by Necator americanus, is a soil-transmitted helminthiasis that disproportionately affects impoverished communities across tropical and subtropical regions, with an estimated 406-480 million people infected globally. Control continues to rely largely on mass drug administration, an approach challenged by rapid reinfection, the absence of durable protective immunity, and growing concern over reduced drug efficacy. While the leading recombinant protein antigens Na-APR-1, Na-GST-1, and Na-ASP-2 have demonstrated clinical safety and immunogenicity, the withdrawal of Na-ASP-2 after triggering allergic reactions in individuals with prior natural exposure revealed both the promise and the risk of single-antigen approaches, underscoring the need for a rationally designed multi-antigen vaccine. We used an immunoinformatics approach to design a novel chimeric vaccine candidate by combining carefully selected B-cell and T-cell epitopes from the major clinical-stage hookworm protein antigens with an immunostimulatory adjuvant sequence. The candidate's 3D structure was predicted, refined, and validated using established bioinformatics approaches, and its interaction with the innate immune receptor TLR4 was assessed through molecular docking and normal-mode analyses. The selected antigens showed conservation across related hookworm species, suggesting the potential for broader cross-protection. The designed candidate was predicted to be antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic, and immune simulation analyses indicated its capacity to elicit coordinated humoral and cellular immune responses. HLA coverage analysis indicated broad population applicability. Docking and normal-mode analyses of its interaction with TLR4 indicated stable and favourable binding. This study offers a rational, safety-driven approach to multi-epitope vaccine design against hookworm infection, integrating the strengths of clinically evaluated protein antigens while addressing the safety concerns raised by prior single-antigen candidates. Further experimental validation is required to confirm the safety and efficacy of the vaccine construct in vitro and in vivo. These findings lay the groundwork for future efforts toward an effective immunoprophylactic strategy against this neglected disease.

papers.title: MOFI reveals dynamic multi-omics coordination during cell fate progression
papers.abstract: Cell fate decisions are shaped by dynamic coordination across transcriptomic, chromatin, and protein layers. Time-series single-cell multi-omics assays now enable these molecular layers to be profiled across developmental stages, yet each cell is still observed only once, and the continuous multi-omics trajectories connecting discrete snapshots remain unresolved. A central challenge is therefore to jointly integrate paired omics measurements while reconstructing their shared developmental progression. Here we present Multi-Omics Fate Inference (MOFI), a dynamically constrained multi-omics integration framework designed to reconstruct continuous cell fate transitions from paired multi-omics snapshots sampled across multiple time points. MOFI jointly models omics-specific state dynamics, cross-omics correspondence, and shared population growth within a unified framework, enabling cross-omics perturbation response analysis and identification of candidate cross-omics transformation programs. Across simulated benchmarks and paired RNA-ATAC/RNA-protein time-series datasets, MOFI reconstructed continuous fate transitions, population dynamics and cross-omics changes consistent with observed measurements. In kidney organoids, MOFI captured coordinated RNA-ATAC progression of nephron lineage specification. In hematopoietic progenitors, MOFI predicted perturbation-responsive lineage redistribution and nominated multi-omics transformation programs linking transcriptional modules with protein-level responses. In neural developmental systems, MOFI resolved gradual brain organoid maturation and interneuron lineage allocation during human cortical development. Together, MOFI provides a dynamics-grounded method for converting discrete paired multi-omics snapshots into interpretable models of cell fate progression, perturbation response, and cross-omics transformation analysis.

papers.title: Clonucopya: An end-to-end workflow bridging tumor clonal architecture and drug prioritization
papers.abstract: Motivation: Intra-tumor heterogeneity limits the effectiveness of anticancer treatments, as distinct clonal populations may respond differently to therapy. Although subclonal inference from sequencing data is well established, translating clonal architecture into actionable drug recommendations remains a major bottleneck. Results: We present Clonucopya, an end-to-end Snakemake workflow that integrates subclonal inference (PyClone-VI, PhyClone) with drug prioritization (PanDrugs2) to link tumor clonal architecture directly to candidate drugs. From genome sequencing data, Clonucopya reconstructs tumor phylogenies, quantifies clone-level prevalence across samples, and ranks FDA/EMA-approved and experimental therapeutic candidates against the somatic mutations detected in each clone. Outputs include clonality plots, per-clone variant and drug tables, and a summary ranking drugs by clonal coverage to highlight broadly active therapeutic candidates. We assess Clonucopya's utility through a real-world longitudinal, multi-region use case, revealing clinically actionable clonal dynamics across tumor progression.

papers.title: Cross-Platform Evaluation of a Tumor-Budding-Associated Gene Signature in Colorectal Cancer.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics has identified AIF1, LIF, MRC1, and TNC as enriched in tumor budding (TB) regions of colorectal cancer. We investigated whether this TB associated gene module could be detected in bulk transcriptomic data. Pairwise gene co-occurrence was analyzed in bulk RNA-seq (TCGA-COADREAD, n=547) and single-cell RNA-seq (GSE178341, n=26,057 cells) using Fisher's exact tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. In bulk RNA-seq, pairwise fold-enrichments were weak (1.16 to 2.72), with AIF1 to LIF showing no significant association (FE=1.16, FDR=0.31). In single-cell data, the same pairs showed 31 to 184.5 fold enrichment (all FDR < 8e-38). Total UMI counts provided no evidence of doublet artifacts explaining these co-detection patterns. Exploratory enhancer-promoter interaction analysis in HCT116 cells further suggested these genes are controlled differently. GOT1 and MDH1, two malate-aspartate shuttle genes, showed lower expression in late-stage CRC (FDR less than or equal to 0.010). A bulk-derived risk score showed a modest association (Cox HR=1.21, p=0.021). Overall, TB-associated co-expression was more clearly detected at single-cell than bulk resolution, highlighting the importance of transcriptomic resolution when studying tumor-microenvironment-associated gene signatures.

papers.title: Scale-resolved correlation functions unify spatial omics across platforms and resolutions
papers.abstract: Spatial omics platforms populate a multidimensional parameter space and differ in resolution, panel size, sensitivity, and modality. This diversity has led to platform-specific analyses whose results are rarely comparable. Here we present SCOTE (Spatial COvariance TEnsors), a computational framework that quantifies spatial relationships of all feature pairs across all length scales, for molecule coordinates and binned counts alike. Measuring the same quantity, with statistical errors, across platforms, samples, and patients, SCOTE separates measurement effects from biology, with platform artifacts appearing as identifiable, scale-localized features. SCOTE's molecule-level functions resolved a knockout effect in mouse spleen that cell-level analyses missed, and could show that tissue area and replicates, not molecule depth, set the statistical error. To match the growth of spatial omics data sets, SCOTE runs efficiently on CPUs and GPUs, and processes a billion-molecule whole-transcriptome section at all length scales, with uncertainties, in 26 minutes on a single GPU.

papers.title: Capturing domain-level detail of molecular interactions in the IMEx Consortium binding domain data set
papers.abstract: The machinery of the cell depends on physical interactions, between proteins themselves, and between proteins and other biomolecules. The detailed characterisation of these interactions, including the identification of the precise sequence regions mediating binding events, is essential to understand both normal cell biology and disease mechanisms. Protein binding domains are specific regions of a protein sequence that mediate direct contact with a partner and represent a critical layer of functional annotation, bridging sequence, structure, and cellular function. Here we present the IMEx binding domain dataset, a large-scale, manually curated open-access set of molecular interactions assembled over more than two decades by the International Molecular Exchange (IMEx) Consortium. The dataset compiles experimentally derived binding region annotations from peer-reviewed literature, systematically linked to protein-protein interaction (PPI) records and mapped to standardised protein sequences in UniProtKB. We describe the curation model, data format, and content of the dataset, provide a descriptive and comparative analysis, and demonstrate the utility of the dataset as a gold standard for benchmarking interface prediction and variant effect annotation methods. Its integration with genomic variations further offers a route to elucidate the mechanistic basis of disease-associated mutations. The datasets are freely available through IntAct in the dedicated PSI-MI FeatureTAB format at https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/intact/current/psimitab/features/ and are updated and enhanced with every release.

papers.title: On technical biases in imaging spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Imaging spatial transcriptomics (iST) has revolutionized our ability to contextualize gene expression within intact tissue architectures at single-cell and subcellular resolution. However, these platforms introduce complex technical biases that span the entire measurement pipeline -- from sample preparation to data acquisition to quantification. Here, we categorize these biases into experimental (e.g., sample preservation and spatial sampling) and computational sources (e.g., z-stack registration and field-of-view stitching). Using public datasets, we demonstrate how different biases can compound and manifest, and propose a unified count modeling framework to formalize these sources of variation. Finally, we call for a more integrated understanding of iST data origins and greater knowledge sharing within and across sectors to support the prospective development of more robust experimental design and reliable downstream analysis.

papers.title: HighFold-Lasso: Topology-Guided Prediction of Lasso Peptide Structures Using AlphaFold3
papers.abstract: Lasso peptides are a class of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) characterized by a mechanically interlocked topology, in which the C-terminal tail is threaded through an N-terminal macrolactam ring formed by an isopeptide bond. This unique topology often confers high thermal stability and resistance to proteolytic degradation. However, the isopeptide linkage, threaded topology, and class-specific disulfide connectivity make lasso peptide structures difficult to reconstruct reliably using general-purpose structure prediction models. Here, we developed HighFold-Lasso, which combines custom covalent connectivity with lasso scaffold-guided adaptive low-noise initialization to enable conditional structure generation guided by lasso conformational priors. On a test set of 52 experimentally determined structures, HighFold-Lasso achieved a 100% lasso topology success rate, with a mean RMSD C-alpha of 1.942 Angstrom for the ring-loop region and 2.375 Angstrom for the full peptide. The framework supports modeling of the four classical lasso peptide classes (I-IV) and can represent noncanonical amino acids, providing computational support for structure-function studies and molecular engineering of lasso peptides.

papers.title: Facilitating Valid Statistical Inference in Biomedical Image Synthesis
papers.abstract: Generative AI for medical image synthesis is increasingly used to impute missing data and augment biomedical datasets. Yet despite achieving high computational similarity to their real-world counterparts, synthetic images remain uncommon in clinical research practice, in part because of concerns about their biological validity. Here, we evaluate whether synthetic images support reliable downstream statistical analysis and biological inference in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and multiplexed immunofluorescence (mIF) imaging. We find that associations between patient phenotypes and synthesized images can be severely attenuated. This is because synthesis methods typically omit clinically relevant covariates and therefore generate images that, although visually realistic, mask key biological differences. Furthermore, naive analyses treat synthesized images as if they were observed, ignoring the statistical uncertainty introduced by synthesis. Drawing on multiple imputation theory, we introduce Phenotype Aware Multiple Synthesis (PAMS), an analysis framework that requires no model retraining and instead adjusts synthesized output to recover valid biological estimates with appropriately calibrated uncertainty. Applied to MRI and mIF data, PAMS reduced estimation bias and restored nominal confidence interval coverage. Because it is compatible with existing synthesis pipelines, PAMS offers a practical and rigorous route to statistically and biologically valid use of synthesized images in biomedical imaging research.

papers.title: Biopsy-aware phylogenetic reconstruction from longitudinal single-cell copy number profiles
papers.abstract: Longitudinal single-cell copy-number profiles provide information about cancer ancestry. Reconstructions that treat all observations as terminal leaves and disregard collection order cannot represent sampled ancestors or use their temporal relationships. We introduce reconstruction methods in the Cancer Tree Biopsy Framework (CTBF) that distinguish a copy-number profile from its separate observations across biopsies. Biopsy-guided reconstruction connects successive samples, defers ambiguous parent assignments, and completes the unresolved ancestry. Partial trees leave unresolved ancestral profiles unspecified. Closed-state trees assign every ancestor an observed profile. For comparison, pooled methods combine the profiles from all biopsies without using collection order. Across 100 independently simulated histories, the biopsy-guided partial methods attained higher mean rooted generalized Robinson--Foulds similarity than pooled neighbor joining and topology-only MEDICC2, using both complete and observed-state-restricted true trees. Under a fixed computational budget, they also attained higher mean similarity than NestedBD-Long at the two evaluated evolutionary depths. Convergence of its Markov chain Monte Carlo runs was not established within that budget. Classical neighbor joining and anticentral top completion gave closely similar partial-tree scores. Closed-state performance depended on evolutionary depth and the evaluation endpoint. An application to three longitudinal KTN152 biopsies demonstrated genome-scale feasibility on patient-derived integer copy-number estimates.

papers.title: Efficient and precise discovery of LTR-retrotransposon families using HiRepEat
papers.abstract: Long Terminal Repeat Retrotransposons (LTR-RTs) are mobile genetic elements that replicate within host genomes using an RNA intermediate. Recent high quality genome assemblies provide new opportunities to study these repetitive elements across evolutionary timescales. We adapt the Myers O(Nd) wavefront alignment algorithm to produce a new fast LTR detection, clustering and phylogenetically-informed consensus approach for identifying LTR-RT families in new genome sequences. We present an iterative approach to identifying and removing repeats, initially tandem repeats, that we call TACO (TAndem COmpressor), and a corresponding coordinate mapping system we call SALSA (Sorted Array for Liftover of Sequence Addresses). Together these allow us to read and write in reduced genome space and search for LTR-RTs and tandem repeats in a series of operations. This greatly reduces confounding between different repeat types and allows us to uncover nested insertions. We show results from our clustering and consensus approach across the >500 genomes in the Vertebrate Genomes Project, with analysis completing in most cases in under 60 minutes with 15Gb memory and 16 cores. We also present cross-genome LTR-RT clustering across 30 Drosophila species, as well as across the VGP, providing fine-grained resolution on species-sharing patterns of LTR-RTs and revealing candidates for horizontal transfer.

papers.title: An integrated data exploration engine of knowledge, expression and genetic association for human transposable elements
papers.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) constitute a substantial fraction of the human genome and contribute to genomic and epigenomic regulation. However, TE-related knowledge remains fragmented across the literature and databases, with inconsistent identifiers hindering integration and reuse. Here, we present TE-Dee (Transposable Element Data Exploration Engine), a curated resource that harmonizes literature-derived TE relationships with TE annotations, tissue-specific expression, and GTEx v11 eQTL associations. TE-Dee contains 10,387 entities and 9,583 curated relationships from 2,308 publications, 1,505 leaf-level TE classification records, and 11,334,060 instance-level observations generated by intersecting 640,456 reference TE intervals with significant variant-gene associations across 50 GTEx tissue categories. By linking molecular knowledge to genomic, transcriptomic and genetic evidence, TE-Dee provides reusable data for investigating TE biology, gene-regulatory and disease-related mechanisms, and a structured corpus for training and benchmarking data-driven and artificial intelligence models. TE-Dee is available at https://bis.zju.edu.cn/tedee/.

papers.title: Non-exonic read content reorganises lncRNA co-expression networks in renal and other cancers
papers.abstract: Co-expression networks are used to find prognostic lncRNA programmes, but lncRNA quantification depends on unprocessed RNA in the library. In renal cancer (1,062 patients), the leading lncRNA axis tracked the non-exonic (non-feature) read fraction, a routine alignment metric, at Spearman rho 0.90. Without adjustment, most of the lncRNA network merged into one module. Adjustment preserved agreement with single-cell tumour-normal differences. Under rules fixed with the renal results known, 9 of 25 TCGA cancer types had a lncRNA-specific axis and 4 had network collapse (8 and 2 of 23 non-renal types). Intronic lncRNAs tracked the metric more than intergenic ones in all 25, and the metric was not consistently prognostic. All five renal modules that survived adjustment kept their direction in an external cohort, two nominally significant and none at a 5% false discovery rate. Three localised to malignant or epithelial cells. Together they added no discrimination over TNM and grade.
